issues.legal_issue: A government decision to disinvest a public-sector undertaking is subject to limited judicial review and may be set aside only for a legally cognizable defect.
material_facts: The government decided to transfer a controlling shareholding and management of a public-sector company to a strategic investor as part of an economic policy.
The sale process included public advertisements, review by government committees, valuation and a reserve price, and acceptance of the highest bid, which exceeded the reserve price.

The petitioners alleged that the process lacked transparency, that the valuation was faulty, and that the accepted price was inadequate, but the Court found no basis to establish arbitrariness, illegality, or an uninformed decision.
issues.conclusion: The disinvestment decision was not invalid, and the Court would not substitute its view on the wisdom of the policy or the valuation for that of the government and its expert bodies.
issues.legal_principle: Economic policy decisions are ordinarily outside the merits review of courts. Judicial review may address whether the decision-maker acted within legal and constitutional limits and whether the process was fair, reasonable, and free from arbitrariness, discrimination, mala fides, or illegality; courts do not decide whether another policy or price would have been wiser. The Court relied on Rustom Cavasjee Cooper v. Union of India; Fertilizer Corporation Kamgar Union v. Union of India; State of M.P. v. Nandlal Jaiswal; R.K. Garg v. Union of India; G.B. Mahajan v. Jalgaon Municipal Council; Peerless General Finance v. Reserve Bank of India; Premium Granites v. State of T.N.; Delhi Science Forum v. Union of India; M.P. Oil Extraction v. State of M.P.; State of Punjab v. Ram Lubhaya Bagga; Bhavesh D. Parish v. Union of India; Narmada Bachao Andolan v. Union of India; and Duncans Industries Ltd. v. State of U.P. on valuation.

rule.if: economic_policy_disinvestment_challenge and transparent_competitive_process and highest_bid_above_reserve and not_evident_arbitrariness and no_shown_legal_violation

predicates.economic_policy_disinvestment_challenge: The proceeding challenges a government decision to transfer control of a public-sector undertaking as an economic policy measure.
predicates.transparent_competitive_process: The government used public notice, competitive participation, and review by responsible decision-making bodies in conducting the sale.
predicates.highest_bid_above_reserve: The government accepted the highest bid, which exceeded the reserve price set for the sale.
predicates.not_evident_arbitrariness: The record does not show that the decision or the sale methodology was plainly arbitrary or irrational.
predicates.no_shown_legal_violation: The challenger has not established that the decision contravened a constitutional or statutory requirement or was mala fide.

issues.definition: When an economic-policy disinvestment challenge concerns a transparent competitive process, the accepted highest bid exceeds the reserve price, and no evident arbitrariness or legal violation is shown, the disinvestment is not invalid.

issues.legal_issue: Workers affected as a class by an economic policy decision have no general right to a pre-decision hearing or continuing consultation before disinvestment.
material_facts: Workers claimed that losing the company’s public-sector status would remove protections associated with constitutional equality and public employment.
They sought consultation at multiple stages, including on whether to disinvest, the choice of strategic partner, and the terms of the sale.
The decision was an executive policy decision, and the Court found no law requiring a hearing before it was made.
issues.conclusion: The workers had no right to a pre-decision hearing or to continuing consultation, and the absence of such a hearing did not by itself invalidate the decision.
issues.legal_principle: Natural justice does not generally require a prior hearing for persons affected as a class by an economic policy decision. A policy decision may still be challenged if it violates law, but the absence of a pre-decisional hearing is not by itself a ground to quash it. The Court relied on State of Haryana v. Des Raj Sangar and distinguished National Textile Workers’ Union v. P.R. Ramakrishnan, which concerned a judicial winding-up proceeding.

predicates.economic_policy_decision: The government made an executive decision about economic policy rather than exercising judicial or quasi-judicial power.
predicates.workers_affected_as_class: The decision affected workers generally through a change in the ownership or management of their employer.
predicates.not_law_requires_prior_hearing: No applicable law required the government to hear the affected workers before making the policy decision.

issues.definition: When an executive economic policy decision affects workers as a class and no law requires a prior hearing, the workers have no general right to be heard before the decision.

issues.legal_issue: A change in shareholding and management does not, by itself, change the employing company or the workers’ employment relationship.
material_facts: A controlling shareholding and management of the company passed to a private strategic investor.
The company itself remained in existence, and its workers continued to be employed by that company.
The sale documents included protections concerning retrenchment and voluntary retirement, and the Court recorded an undertaking concerning continued employment subject to applicable rules and law.
issues.conclusion: The change in management did not amount in law to a change of employer or employment, and the workers’ employment relationship remained with the company.
issues.legal_principle: A transfer of shares and control of a company does not, without more, transfer the company’s employees to a different employer: the company remains the employer. The Court also referred to protections under the Industrial Disputes Act and the company’s certified service conditions.

predicates.share_control_changes: A new shareholder acquires control of a company and its management.
predicates.company_continues_as_employer: The company remains in existence and continues to employ the same workers.

issues.definition: When control changes but the company continues to employ the workers, their employment relationship with the company is unchanged.

issues.legal_issue: A government is not bound to follow an advisory body’s earlier recommendation on the extent of a proposed disinvestment.
material_facts: An advisory commission initially recommended selling a minority share to a strategic partner and reducing the government’s remaining holding later.
The government’s governing resolution made the commission advisory and reserved the final decision to the government.
The commission’s chair later advised that a controlling shareholding could be offered, and the government proceeded on that advice.
issues.conclusion: The government’s decision to sell a controlling shareholding was not an unlawful or arbitrary departure from the commission’s earlier recommendation.
issues.legal_principle: Where an advisory body’s recommendations are non-binding and the government retains final decision-making authority, the government may make a different decision, including in light of subsequent advice. The Court considered the government resolutions governing the Disinvestment Commission and its recommendations and the chair’s later advice.

predicates.disinvestment_recommendation_is_advisory: The body making the recommendation has an advisory rather than binding role.
predicates.government_retains_final_authority: The government’s governing arrangement reserves the final decision to the government.
predicates.later_advice_supports_sale: Subsequent advice from the advisory body’s chair supports the form of sale the government chooses.

issues.definition: When a disinvestment recommendation is advisory, the government retains final authority, and later advice supports the sale, a departure from the earlier recommendation does not invalidate the decision.

issues.legal_issue: A change in the ownership or management of a company does not itself create a fresh transfer of land previously validly granted to that company.
material_facts: Land had been acquired or leased to the company under the applicable state land law, and the required permission for transfers of private land had been granted.
The applicable state law did not absolutely prohibit the relevant lease to a non-tribal entity and expressly excluded leases from the relevant restriction after amendment.
The land remained with the same company after its shareholding and management changed; it was not transferred to a different company.
issues.conclusion: The disinvestment did not constitute a new transfer of land or invalidate the earlier grant, and the decision in Samatha v. State of A.P. did not apply because the governing statutory provisions were different.
issues.legal_principle: Section 165(6) of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959, as applicable to the land grants, did not impose the same absolute prohibition as section 3(1) of the Andhra Pradesh Scheduled Areas Land Transfer Regulation, 1959. Samatha v. State of A.P. was therefore distinguishable. A change in shareholding or management does not itself transfer land from the company to another entity. The Court also referred to Article 145(3) of the Constitution in discussing the interpretation of constitutional provisions in Samatha.

predicates.land_previously_validly_granted_to_compa: The land was previously granted or transferred to the company in accordance with the applicable law.
predicates.company_retains_land: The same company continues to hold the land after the challenged transaction.
predicates.only_shareholding_or_management_changes: The transaction changes ownership or management of the company without transferring the land to another entity.

issues.definition: When land was validly granted to a company, the company retains it, and only its shareholding or management changes, no new land transfer occurs.

issues.legal_issue: A stranger’s public-interest petition challenging a government’s economic policy decision is not maintainable merely because the decision is said to affect the public.
material_facts: The petitioner was neither an employee of the company nor a prospective bidder in the sale.
He challenged the government’s economic policy decision as a public-interest litigant.
The Court found no basis to treat the petition as one brought on behalf of disadvantaged people unable to approach the court or to establish the relevant violation of fundamental rights.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to entertain the public-interest petition.
issues.legal_principle: Public-interest litigation is principally a means to protect the rights of disadvantaged people who cannot effectively seek relief themselves, and it must be brought bona fide by a person with sufficient interest. It is not a vehicle for a stranger to challenge an economic or financial policy decision. The Court relied on S.P. Gupta v. Union of India; Sachidanand Pandey v. State of West Bengal; Subhash Kumar v. State of Bihar; Janata Dal v. H.S. Chowdhary; Raunaq International Ltd. v. I.V.R. Construction Ltd.; and Narmada Bachao Andolan v. Union of India.

rule.if: public_interest_litigation and petitioner_is_stranger_to_decision and economic_policy_challenge and no_unable_disadvantaged_group_or_rights_violation_shown

predicates.public_interest_litigation: The proceeding is brought as a public-interest petition rather than as a personal claim by an affected party.
predicates.petitioner_is_stranger_to_decision: The petitioner is neither personally affected in the relevant capacity nor a participant in the challenged transaction.
predicates.economic_policy_challenge: The petition challenges a government decision concerning economic or financial policy.
predicates.no_unable_disadvantaged_group_or_rights_: The petition does not establish that it is brought for disadvantaged people unable to approach the court or that the relevant fundamental-rights violation has occurred.

issues.definition: When a stranger brings a public-interest petition against an economic policy decision without showing that it protects an unable disadvantaged group or addresses a relevant rights violation, the petition is not entertained.

issues.legal_issue: A constitutional petition challenging show-cause notices should not be entertained when an adequate statutory remedy is available.
material_facts: The company challenged show-cause notices issued by government authorities under applicable laws.
Those laws provided the company with an adequate remedy, and the company could also approach the appropriate High Court in a suitable case.
issues.conclusion: The Court did not entertain the constitutional petition because an alternative remedy was available.
issues.legal_principle: The Court declined to exercise its constitutional jurisdiction to address the show-cause notices where the petitioner had an adequate remedy under the laws pursuant to which the notices were issued, including recourse to the High Court in an appropriate case.

predicates.constitutional_petition_against_show_cau: The proceeding invokes constitutional jurisdiction to challenge a show-cause notice issued under a statutory scheme.
predicates.adequate_statutory_remedy_available: The governing law provides an adequate means to contest the notice, including an available route to a competent court in an appropriate case.

issues.definition: When a constitutional petition challenges a show-cause notice and an adequate statutory remedy is available, the petition is not entertained.
